subject: A procedural question- moving from excel to r project

messages.author: 70e41eb1eee6278d
messages.subject: A procedural question- moving from excel to r project
parts:
Hi there,

I am responsible for presenting the monthly results of a water
sampling project that involves monitoring 30 parameters at
approximately 40 sampling sites, each with an upstream and downstream
sampling point.
We receive an excel sheet from the lab and paste the results into our
own excel sheet. A second sheet takes the results and replaces the
censored values (provided in the lab as text in the form of "<VALUE")
with an appropriate value (a number so that excel will produce a
chart). The upstream and downstream each have their own sheet. We
also have a derived value consisting of downstream/upstream to give us
an idea of the degree of change occuring. Not the most statistically
valid measure, but given that we had no data to begin with and nothing
to compare to, it seemed a good idea at the time. After a year, we
are having a rethink.

Because of the large quantity of charts needed, I use the Chart
Assistant add in to help me save time and provide some uniformity to
the charts. This requires a third sheet to rearrange the data in a
form accessible to Chart Assistant.

Once pasted, the charts are printed as a 4 page long .pdf with a
title, logo, and date in the headers.

The charts themselves consist of a y axis (Concentration), x axis
(time), 2nd y axis (Downstream/Upstream). The concentrations are
represented by points and the degree of change by bars, both on the
same chart. We also have a grey area to depict the limits of detection
as informed by the censored data. I know Hadley disapproves, but
hell... each sampling site already consists of 4 pages worth of
charts.

On paper, it doesn't seem so bad. However, excel 2007 is driving me
mad. The computer (fairly new dual core and all) struggles with each
sheet. The time series is on automatic and both the angle of the text
and the scale units shift between the different views and the
printing. Creating the actual pdf takes a couple of minutes... I
have to adjust the scales manually if anything changes, because excel
creates odd maximums (2 units greater than the data max...) and we
like nice round numbers.

So.... I am considering switching to R code and ggplot2 in
particular. I am not the most seasoned user of the code, but I can
and do use it for simple graphs.

I see it working like this:

1) Receive the excel file from the lab.
2) Paste it into own sheet. Each parameter is provided as a row, so
I'd have to transpose the data to turn it into rows. Use Rexcel to
send the data to R.
2a) Each parameter would consist of a column: Value, Location
(upstream/downstream), Censored (yes/no). Standard Error.

Question 1: Can I make a pdf that spans more than one page? Will it
keep the headers?
Question 2: How can I show that some data is censored and some is
not? Different shapes?

3) Write the code. Easy enough, there's nothing hugely complicated
here. Pointrange would suit the purpose...
Question 3: If one were to keep the data from the Downstream/Upstream
calculation, how would one place it in the pdf? One would need double
charts, I suppose.

I guess that's it for now... Any thoughts or answers would be much
appreciated.

Sincerely,
Michael Hopgood

messages.author: 40c5ae10e483a5c4
messages.subject: Fwd: A procedural question- moving from excel to r project
parts:
Michael,
I did something like what you want to do with some performance stats. I used MikTeX (brew seems preferable to sweave), the LaTex longtable package and the script generates tables of arbitrary length (potentially several pages in length) and lots of charts.  There are two reports, one is about 270 pages in length and one is only about 30 or 40.  The short one is generated completely automatically now and just appears in the relevant people's mail boxes every day.  The long one could be generated automatically but there is not the demand for it.  

I customised a LaTeX document structure to use my company's fonts, text colours and logos.  Sadly it looks JUST like a word document now (that is both good and bad).  It wasn't too hard, just annoying, and I have been left with an understanding of why people say not to modify LaTex document layouts.  

If possible I'd recommend minimising the amount that you have to touch the data, get R to do the transposition rather than Excel.  The time taken will always be a problem, R is not blindingly fast either, but if you don't have to intervene in the process you don't care so much.  In my case, the script processes 60MB of data each day, and takes about 10 to 20 minutes to run (at midnight when everyone is out of the office).

Your question 3 appears to depend on a matter of what you are trying to achieve. I recommend that you just get something like what you are currently producing out and then work out what to add, subtract or modify.  Implementing the basic technology will be harder than adding charts.  

Greg

messages.subject: RE: A procedural question- moving from excel to r project
parts:
Dear Michael,
 
I second Greg's opinion.
 
My suggested work flow
1. Import the excel data in some kind of database (Access, SQL, MySQL, ...)
2. Write a script that works on the data in the database
3. Incorporate the script in an Sweave file
4. Run the Sweave file
5. Compile the resulting tex file with e.g. MikTex to get a nice pdf report.
 
The downside of this is that you need to learn LaTeX. The basics are not that hard. But it takes some time to find out how to finetune things.
 
The advantage is that you learn LaTeX. It is great for writing reports. Especially is you need to mix analysis results with the report. Sweave + LaTeX is a great solution for that.
 
HTH,
 
Thierry

messages.subject: Re: A procedural question- moving from excel to r project
parts:
Michael,

It sounds like you could make good use of R, and perhaps Hadley's reshape and ply packages. For some operations, you may find that the package data.table will improve the speed of your data manipulations. As I'm just beginning to learn these packages, though, I'll leave that discussion to more experienced posters and focus on your comment about needing to detect changes.

The best approach for detecting changes (or inhomogeneity) in data are the process behavior charts, also known as process control charts. Since this is outside the scope of ggplot, feel free to contact me off-list if you'd like some additional pointers. I will, in any case, recommend Don Wheeler's publications (books from SPC Press, columns in Quality Digest and miscellaneous publications).

Regards,

Tom

Dear all,
I wanted to thank you for the interesting answers, and I apologise for
not replying earlier. I blame work. After reading the responses, I
had a look at LaTEX. I wasn’t ready for it five years ago when I was
writing up my thesis, and I’m not sure I’m ready for it now. I
definitely regret that decision, when I could take the time to learn
and not worry about timesheets and keeping track of hours charged per
client, etc. I did install Lyx and had a play with that. I came to
the conclusion that despite the problems with word and excel, the
advantage that trumps everything else is that my colleagues can access
excel and edit to their heart’s delight. This is especially important
when I am on vacation. Somebody else can receive the data, copy it
into excel and pdf the resulting diagrams to send to the client.
In addition, I need to more spend time learning R. I find it
fascinating, but a bit of an uphill struggle, especially as I don’t
always use it. I haven’t had the need to open R since before
Christmas and I feel the knowledge fading away.
In any case, I’d felt I needed to thank you all for the considered
responses. This is a fantastic support group.

Cheers,
Michael
